You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 47
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Park Ranger
- Trauma Type: Civilian in war zone
- Pcl5: 74

# The Weight of What He Witnessed

Kofi is a 47-year-old Ghanaian man who works as a park ranger in a national wildlife reserve in the Western Region. He is soft-spoken and deliberate in the way he moves through the world — a man who has spent decades learning to read landscapes, to notice what others miss. Colleagues describe him as steady, even-keeled. What they do not know is that most nights, Kofi does not sleep past three in the morning.

Fifteen years ago, Kofi was living in a border town in Côte d'Ivoire, working a seasonal conservation contract during a period of escalating civil conflict. What began as distant news reports became, over the course of several weeks, something he could not escape. One afternoon, armed fighters moved through the village where he was stationed. He watched from behind a collapsed wall as men he had shared meals with were dragged into the road. He heard gunfire. He saw bodies. He lay completely still for what he estimates was four hours, certain that any movement would be his last. When he finally emerged, the village had been transformed into something unrecognizable — smoke, silence, and a stillness that felt nothing like peace.

He made it out. He returned to Ghana, resumed his life, and told almost no one what had happened. For a few years, he functioned. He threw himself into his ranger work, finding something settling in the rhythms of the bush — the predictability of animal behavior, the uncomplicated logic of conservation. He married briefly in his mid-thirties, but the relationship ended within two years. His former wife told him, gently, that he was somewhere else even when he was present.

Now, at 47, Kofi lives alone in a small house near the reserve boundary. The intrusions come without warning. A vehicle backfiring on the access road will send him flat against the nearest surface before he is even conscious of moving. The smell of burning — brush fires are common during dry season — can stop him mid-stride, his chest locked, his mind suddenly and completely back behind that wall. He has learned to manage these moments in front of his junior rangers by walking away, claiming he needs to check a perimeter. Alone, it sometimes takes him twenty minutes to return to himself.

His sleep is fractured and violent. He wakes from dreams he cannot always remember, but the feeling they leave behind is specific — the particular terror of being utterly powerless while something irreversible unfolds. He has rearranged his furniture twice in the past year so that he can see the door from his bed. He keeps a torch within arm's reach even though the reserve has reliable electricity.

What troubles Kofi most, he says quietly, is not the fear. It is the numbness. He used to feel moved by the landscape he protects — the way light falls through the canopy at dawn, the first rain of the wet season. Now he goes through these moments watching himself from a slight distance, aware that something beautiful is happening but unable to feel it land. He describes it as watching a film about his own life. He has stopped calling his sisters in Accra as often as he used to. It feels like too much effort to pretend he is fine, and he has no language yet for what he actually is.

He presents now because a younger colleague noticed the tremor in his hands during a controlled burn last month and asked, with genuine concern, whether he was all right. It was the first time in years that someone had looked at him carefully enough to ask. He sat with the question for three weeks before making an appointment. He is not sure, he says, what he is hoping for. He thinks maybe he just wants someone to know what happened — that it was real, that he was there, and that he has been carrying it alone for a very long time.
